name: Asante (Ashanti) Empire
summary: An Akan state in present-day Ghana, united by the Golden Stool. It grew rich from gold and trade and fought five wars against Britain.

knownFor.label: Golden Stool
knownFor.note: Sacred throne said to hold the soul of the Asante nation; never sat on.

knownFor.label: Kente cloth
knownFor.note: Brightly woven strips of cloth worn by royalty, now a symbol of Ghana.

knownFor.label: Akan gold weights
knownFor.note: Small cast-brass figures used to weigh gold dust, often showing proverbs.

knownFor.label: Asante musketeers
knownFor.note: Large disciplined armies armed with imported muskets.

location.value: Southern and central Ghana, ruled from Kumasi.

terrain.value: Tropical forest in the south, opening to savannah in the north.
terrain.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

climate.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

resources.value: Gold, kola nuts, and fertile forest farmland.
resources.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

disasters.value: No specific natural disasters are recorded.
disasters.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

population.value: About 3–4 million in the 19th century (estimates vary).
population.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

urbanisation.value: Kumasi was a large capital with wide streets and royal buildings.
urbanisation.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

disease.value: Malaria, which also killed many European soldiers.
disease.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

migration.value: War captives were incorporated or sold; traders came from the Muslim north.
migration.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

economicBase.value: Gold, agricultural exports, craft work, northern trade and slave trading.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

tradeRoutes.value: North to Hausa and Sahel markets (kola nuts); south to European forts on the coast (gold, captives).
tradeRoutes.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

moneyAndTax.value: Gold dust, weighed with small cast-brass weights.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

inequality.value: Royals and chiefs above commoners; slaves at the bottom.
inequality.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

keyRulers.value: Osei Tutu (founder, with priest Okomfo Anokye), Opoku Ware I, Osei Bonsu, Prempeh I (exiled 1896).
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

succession.value: The queen mother nominated a candidate from the royal lineage; councils approved.
succession.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

stability.value: A strong central state with a council and assembly; regional revolts at times.
stability.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

eliteConflict.value: Unknown in detail; rivalries between chiefs and the Asantehene at times.
eliteConflict.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

armyAndTech.value: Large armies of musketeers, organised in advance guard, main body and wings.
armyAndTech.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

majorWars.value: Conquest of Denkyira (1701), wars with the Fante, and five Anglo-Ashanti Wars (1823–1900).
majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

territoryChange.value: Expanded across most of modern Ghana in the 18th century; area about 259,000 km².
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Denkyira, the Fante confederation and Britain; traded with the Dutch.
alliancesRivals.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

inventions.value: Akan brass gold-weights, cast in the shapes of animals and proverbs.
inventions.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

scienceEducation.value: Little is known; knowledge was kept by court officials and in oral tradition.
scienceEducation.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

openness.value: Traded with Europeans while resisting their rule.
openness.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

communicationTransport.value: The “Great Roads” radiating from Kumasi, with messengers and toll points.

religion.value: Akan religion: Nyame (the sky god), lesser gods and ancestors.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

languageWriting.value: Asante Twi; Arabic used by Muslim scribes.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

artsArchitecture.value: Asante traditional buildings (a UNESCO World Heritage Site), kente cloth and goldwork.
artsArchitecture.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

socialStructure.value: Royals, chiefs, commoners and slaves, organised in matrilineal clans.
socialStructure.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

sharedIdentity.value: The Golden Stool, said to have descended from the sky, is the soul of the nation.
sharedIdentity.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

dailyLife.value: Courtyard buildings with decorated walls (now a World Heritage Site); yams, plantain, fufu and palm-nut soup.

neighbours.value: Fante, Denkyira, Dagomba, the British and Dutch.
neighbours.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

ideasReligions.value: Islam spread among traders in the north.
ideasReligions.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

colonisation.value: Annexed by Britain; part of the Gold Coast colony from 1 January 1902.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

riseSignals.value: Osei Tutu united the Akan states and defeated Denkyira in 1701.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

peakPeriod.value: Early 19th century, at its largest extent.
peakPeriod.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

declineSignals.value: Wars with Britain; Kumasi was burnt in 1874.
declineSignals.source: Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

outcome.value: Became part of the British Gold Coast in 1902. The Asante kingdom survives today as a traditional state within Ghana.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Asante Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Wilks, Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

sources.value: Oral history. Checked against Wikipedia (“Asante Empire”).

overallCertainty.value: Good. Asante oral history and European records broadly agree. Second source: Wikidata gives 1670 (the Kumasi state before the empire); Wikipedia’s infobox gives 1701.
